title: Your left lung is smaller than your right, to make room for your heart
body: The right lung has three lobes and the left only two, and the left is the smaller of the pair because it shares the left side of the chest with the heart, with an indentation called the cardiac notch to accommodate it. Together the lungs weigh about 1.3 kg and contain some **300 to 500 million alveoli**, the tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood. Folded into the chest, that surface adds up to an estimated 50 to 75 square metres, dozens of times the area of your skin, reached through roughly 2,400 km of branching airways.

cover.alt: A normal chest X-ray seen from the front, showing both lungs as dark areas inside the ribcage and the heart's pale shadow on the left side

slides.question: How many lobes does each lung have?
slides.explanation: The right lung has three lobes and the left two. The left lung also has a cardiac notch, an indentation in its border that makes room for the heart.

slides.heading: Surface area, in square metres
slides.note: Skin averages 1.5 to 2 m²; estimates of total lung surface area range from 50 to 75 m²

slides.question: How long are all the airways in your lungs, laid end to end?
slides.explanation: Approximately 2,400 km of airways branch from the windpipe down to the alveoli, the 300 to 500 million tiny sacs where gas exchange happens.

slides.alt: A coronal CT scan slice of the chest showing both lungs in black with branching airways, and the heart between them
slides.caption: A CT slice through the chest. The heart sits mostly to the left, which is why the left lung is smaller and has only two lobes.

slides.heading: Heavier on the right
slides.text: Both lungs together weigh about 1.3 kg, and the right is the heavier. Reference ranges run from roughly 155 to 720 g for a man's right lung and 110 to 675 g for his left, with women's lungs a little lighter.
